sysd-reliab-106.title: Hash function: any input, one fixed-size value
sysd-reliab-106.text: Feed a hash function a short word or a very long document and it hands back a value of the same fixed size. People call that value a hash value, hash code, digest or simply a hash. Usually it indexes a table of data, a structure with its own entry, {{ref:sysd-blocks-182}}. Retrieval then takes small, nearly constant time. A good function does three jobs. It folds variable-length keys into fixed-length values, scrambles the bits so values spread uniformly, and maps them into the size of the table. It must be fast and deterministic, so the same input always gives the same value. That rules out anything that depends on a random number generator or the time of day. Pathological keys, a poor design or a crowded table can still push access time toward linear. A hash function is also an essential ingredient of {{ref:sysd-reliab-001}}.

sysd-reliab-117.title: Base64: carrying binary data as plain text
sysd-reliab-117.text: Some channels carry only text, and a photo is not text. Base64 is the workaround: a binary-to-text encoding that represents each 6-bit segment of the data with one of 64 printable characters. Four characters stand for every three input bytes, so the encoded data is 33% larger, plus about 3% more if line breaks are inserted. When the input is not a multiple of three bytes, the last group is padded with = characters, one after two leftover bytes and two after one. The alphabet is A-Z, a-z and 0-9 for the first 62 values. Many variants add + and / for the last two, and RFC 4648 describes the most common one. Base64 embeds images in HTML, CSS and XML. It also carries e-mail attachments, because SMTP was originally designed to transport only 7-bit ASCII. Not every system follows RFC 4648: Unix crypt does not, and neither does the scheme in {{ref:sysd-reliab-122}}.

sysd-reliab-107.title: Hash collision: when two inputs share one value
sysd-reliab-107.text: Two different inputs can end up with the same hash value. That is a hash collision, and it is not a bug but a certainty. Hash functions are many-to-one, with far more possible inputs than output values. With more objects than hash values, the pigeonhole principle guarantees a collision. The birthday paradox makes collisions likely long before the output range is used up. A birthday attack exploits this: finding any two inputs that collide is easier than matching one specific value. Cryptographic hash functions are designed so that finding a collision is computationally infeasible. Simple checks such as CRC have essentially no such resistance, so they cannot protect input an attacker can manipulate. A table indexed by hash values copes with open addressing, which probes for another empty cell, or with separate chaining, which keeps a linked list in each cell. Whether collisions hurt depends on the job: checksums try to avoid them between similar inputs, while hashes built to find similar data want them.

sysd-reliab-001.title: Bloom filter: a set that answers maybe or never
sysd-reliab-001.text: A Bloom filter answers "have I seen this before?" with either "definitely not" or "probably yes". It is a space-efficient probabilistic data structure that tests whether an element is in a set, allowing false positives but never false negatives. It is a bit array of m bits, all 0 at first, plus k hash functions. Adding an element sets to 1 the k positions its hashes select. To test an element, check those positions. Any 0 means it is definitely absent. All 1s mean it is present, or that other elements set those bits by chance. The false positive rate climbs as items are added, until every bit is 1 and every query answers positive. The bargain is thrifty. With an optimal number of hash functions, a 1% false positive rate takes only about 9.6 bits per element, whatever its size, because the filter stores no items. Cassandra, HBase and PostgreSQL use Bloom filters to skip disk lookups for missing rows.

sysd-reliab-006.title: Quadtree: cutting space into four, again and again
sysd-reliab-006.text: Measuring the distance from one point to every other point does not scale. Finding how close points are with latitude, longitude and Euclidean distance is CPU-intensive on large data sets. A quadtree avoids that work. It is a tree in which each internal node has exactly four children. It partitions two-dimensional space by recursively subdividing it into four quadrants or regions, and each child or leaf stores spatial information. Searching for points within a two-dimensional range then becomes efficient. Subdividing a node only after a size threshold saves computation, and a mapping such as {{ref:sysd-reliab-115}} can improve range query performance further. Quadtrees are the two-dimensional analog of octrees, which partition three-dimensional space. They serve spatial indexing and range queries, location-based services such as Google Maps and Uber, image processing and compression, mesh generation and sparse data storage.

sysd-reliab-110.title: MD5: a famous hash that collisions broke
sysd-reliab-110.text: MD5 turns a message of any length into a 128-bit hash value, typically written as 32 hexadecimal digits. It pads the message and processes it in 512-bit blocks, and the avalanche effect means a small change gives a mostly different hash. Yet in 2004 MD5 was shown not to be collision-resistant. Collisions can now be found within seconds, and the CMU Software Engineering Institute calls it cryptographically broken. It is unsuitable for SSL certificates or digital signatures. An MD5 checksum can still reveal a corrupt or incomplete download, but it cannot protect against deliberate tampering.

sysd-reliab-116.title: K-d tree: splitting space one axis at a time
sysd-reliab-116.text: A k-d tree finds the stored point nearest to a query without checking every one. It is a space-partitioning data structure, a binary tree whose nodes are points, for organizing points in a k-dimensional space. Each non-leaf node implicitly defines a splitting hyperplane perpendicular to one of the k axes. Points on one side go to the left subtree and points on the other side to the right. In the canonical construction the splitting axis cycles as you go down and each node takes the median point on that axis, which yields a balanced tree. Nearest-neighbor search descends as if inserting the query point, saves the leaf's point as the current best, then unwinds, updating the best at each node. At each node it asks whether a hypersphere around the query crosses the splitting plane, with the current best distance as radius. If not, that whole branch is eliminated. In low dimensions this takes O(log n) on average. In high dimensions the curse of dimensionality makes the search no better than exhaustive search.

sysd-reliab-113.title: Trie: a tree that spells out its keys
sysd-reliab-113.text: Type the first letters of a word and a list of completions appears. Tries are built for that kind of lookup. A trie, also called a prefix tree or digital tree, is a search tree for storing and retrieving strings from a dictionary or set. Its nodes do not store their keys. A node's position determines its key, edges stand for single characters, every child shares a common prefix with its parent, and the root represents the empty string. Searching follows the key's characters from the root, and a null link means the key does not exist. The search takes O(m) time, where m is the length of the key. A trie needs no hash function, has no collisions and sorts keys lexicographically. The cost is memory: each node has as many links as the alphabet has characters, 128 for ASCII, and most are null. A radix tree, or compressed trie, merges any node with only one child into its parent to save space. Tries suit autocomplete, spell checking and longest-prefix matching in IP routing, because lookups follow prefixes.

sysd-reliab-114.title: Z-order curve: flattening many dimensions into one
sysd-reliab-114.text: How do you put points from a map into one list so that neighbors stay neighbors? The Z-order, or Morton, curve is one answer. It maps multidimensional data to one dimension while preserving locality: points close together in several dimensions usually lie close together in the order. The z-value of a point comes from interleaving the bits of its binary coordinates. Connecting the values in numerical order draws a recursively Z-shaped curve. Once the data are sorted this way, any one-dimensional structure can hold them, and a balanced tree handles dynamic data with O(log n) insertion and deletion. The order equals a depth-first traversal of a quadtree, so the points in any quadtree square form a contiguous interval. A range query cannot simply use binary search. From the z-value reached, the search computes the next z-value inside the range and skips the stretch between. Z-order is one of the few multidimensional access methods in commercial data stores. A rival with better order-preserving behavior is {{ref:sysd-reliab-115}}, while {{ref:sysd-reliab-005}} is based on Z-order.

sysd-reliab-005.title: Geohash: a place as a short string
sysd-reliab-005.text: In a geohash, the longer two places' codes agree at the start, the closer the places are. A geohash encodes latitude and longitude into a short alphanumeric string. It is a hierarchical spatial index in a Base-32 alphabet: its first character identifies one of 32 cells, and that cell in turn contains 32 cells. The world is recursively divided into smaller cells with each additional bit until the desired precision is reached. A longer string therefore means a smaller cell and a more precise location. The codes 9q8yy9mf and 9q8yy9vx are close because they share the prefix 9q8yy9. A geohash is a plain string, so a location is easy to store in a data store column. Nearest neighbors can then be found with simple string comparisons and efficient index searches. The scheme applies the Z-order curve, and removing characters from the end gradually reduces both the code size and the precision. Depending on its length, a geohash tells only that a user is somewhere within an area, which gives a degree of anonymity.

sysd-reliab-115.title: Hilbert curve: a space-filling curve that keeps neighbors near
sysd-reliab-115.text: In 1891 David Hilbert first described a continuous space-filling fractal curve that now carries his name. The Hilbert curve maps between one and two dimensions while preserving locality fairly well: points that are close in one dimension stay close after folding. That property is why the curve is widely used in computer science, including to index geospatial location data. Singh's Uber design applies mapping algorithms such as the Hilbert curve to run range queries that find nearby drivers. For multidimensional data the Hilbert order has also been proposed instead of Z order, because it preserves locality better.

sysd-reliab-109.title: Similarity hashing: when similar data should collide
sysd-reliab-109.text: A cryptographic hash is built so that even a tiny change gives a very different value. Similarity hashing, also called fuzzy hashing, does the opposite: it produces hashes that show when data is similar but not identical. A perceptual hash fingerprints multimedia and is a type of locality-sensitive hash, so similar features give similar hashes. It is used to find online copyright infringement and in digital forensics. Hashes meant to find similar data, such as homologous DNA sequences or similar audio files, are designed to maximize collisions between similar items. Fuzzy hashing has also been used to identify malware.

sysd-reliab-108.title: String hashing: folding text into a number
sysd-reliab-108.text: Strings have very uneven distributions, which makes them awkward to hash. String hashing folds the characters of a variable-length string into a fixed-size hash code. A common fold multiplies a running total by a sizable prime constant, adds the next character and ignores overflow. A modulo or mask then fits the result to the table. Information can cluster in the upper or lower bits of the bytes, because ASCII codes have a top bit of 0, for example. That clustering survives into the hash and causes more collisions. Hashing only the first and last characters saves iterating over the string, but such functions can readily become linear.

sysd-reliab-008.title: Distributed unique ID generation: many machines, no clashes
sysd-reliab-008.text:
Many machines must hand out IDs at the same moment, and no two IDs may ever match. A distributed unique ID generator produces globally unique numerical IDs that are roughly sorted by time and generated at low latency by many machines. In social media, IDs should be roughly sorted by time, numerical only, and highly scalable with low latency. Each generator has its own pros and cons.

A UUID has 128 bits and is simple to generate without calling another service. It is not sequential, though, and it is inefficient for indexing in a data store. ID conflicts, though unlikely, are possible. The Snowflake scheme builds an ID from a timestamp, a machine ID and a serial number, with the first bit unused so IDs stay positive. It needs no network call to an ID service, so it is fast and scalable. Implementations vary: a data center ID can be added to the machine ID component to guarantee global uniqueness.

A data store's auto-increment column uses its transaction management to handle concurrent requests and guarantees uniqueness within one table. It needs network communication, and as user IDs it may expose sensitive business data, giving competitors a rough idea of the total number of registered users. In the segment approach, ID servers fetch IDs from the data store in batches and cache them, each server handling a segment of IDs. That greatly saves I/O pressure. The store described in {{ref:sysd-blocks-029}} can also generate unique IDs from a key-value pair, and because it keeps data in memory this performs better than the data store approach.
